rv.q: Gradually, the play reveals itself as a touching celebration of enduring love, family and forgiveness.
And what an unexpected treat it is.
What unfolds is an extraordinary evening of domestic time travel – a marvel – in which we are taken back to the 30s and into a grand English house outside Birmingham with sage green walls.
This glorious revival of Dodie Smith’s interwar family drama is a visual and emotional feast.
It is what it is: a slightly soppy, unfashionable play whose 90 years are showing.

But for all its occasional longueurs, the evening is lifted by an imperious performance by Lindsay Duncan as a grandmother presiding over golden anniversary celebrations that come close to being thrown off course by domestic tensions and romantic intrigues.
A gorgeous evening that deserves to spread its tentacles further than this limited run.
And yet it's been some while since I so fully and happily surrendered to a bygone world laced with warmth, wit, and a clear-eyed worldliness that keeps sentimentality at bay.

cn.t: Dodie Smith's 1938 family drama receives a timely, poignant revival anchored by Lindsay Duncan's superb performance. Critics find the old-fashioned play surprisingly resonant, with its melancholy tone reflecting contemporary anxieties.
